newsitem.title: BELGIUM: FOCUS-EU's Van Miert ups pressure on Boeing.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-EU's Van Miert ups pressure on Boeing.

text.p: European Competition Commissioner Karel Van Miert stepped up pressure on Boeing Co on Tuesday saying he would not accept the proposed merger with McDonnell Douglas Corp as it currently stands.

The European Commission has the power to vet mergers or acquisitions involving companies that make over 250 million ECUs in sales in the European Union and with a combined global turnover of five billion ECUs.

Van Miert's statement was a clear signal that he would not change his negative opinion of the deal no matter what political pressure was applied from the United States, home of the two aircraft manufacturers, EU sources said.

He also strongly rejected accusations led by U.S. Senator Slade Gorton that the Commission was not being "objective" in its assessment of the merger and was defending the interests of Airbus Industrie -- a consortium of powerful aircraft manufacturers in France, Germany, Britain and Spain which provides the main competition for Boeing.
"Our analysis of the Boeing-McDonnell Douglas file is conducted strictly on the basis of the European merger regulation, and nothing else," he said in a statement.
Senator Gorton of Washington, where Boeing is based, wrote to U.S. President Bill Clinton last week urging him to ensure a fair EU review.
Boeing's vice president for EU affairs Jim Frank told Reuters he had no complaints about the way the Commission's merger task-force has been handling the case.
"So far we have not had any signs that the merger task-force would not do its work as one would expect," Frank told Reuters from Boeing's office in Brussels.
He declined to comment on the concessions sought by the Commission, but reiterated the company's belief that the deal did not dramatically change the state of competition in the aircraft industry.
The EU's merger regulations empower the Commission to rule whether the merger of the two companies creates or strengthens a dominant position in the 15-nation Union.

Boeing alone currently has a 60-percent share of the overall world market for commercial jets and this would increase with the control of McDonnell, the Commission said in March after an initial one-month review of the merger.
Boeing argues that the increase would only be minimal given that McDonnell is mainly active in the defence and space business and its small commercial aircraft activity has substantially declined.

Van Miert said in Tuesday's statement he expected the companies to offer formal remedies to his concerns after the Commission has detailed its grievances in a so-called statement of objections. This would be sent before the end of May.
"The initiation of such an in-depth inquiry clearly demonstrates that, in its present form, this merger case is not in line with the European merger regulation," Van Miert said.
"In this document which will be sent to the companies involved in this merger case, we will clearly point out all the elements that cause our deep worries," he said.
"As usual we expect the recipient companies to offer formal remedies to the worries expressed."

Van Miert has expressed concern about the greater leverage the group would have in negotiating exclusive contracts with airlines, following Boeing deals agreed by Delta Air Lines and AMR Corp.'s American Airlines.
He has said such contracts were unacceptable, but Boeing argues that the Commission has no jurisdiction to intervene in commercial decisions between non-EU companies.
The deadline for the Commission's decision on whether to clear the merger is on July 31.
The alliance is also being investigated by the U.S. Federal Trade Commission.
